blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

Most first-round problems are about *remembering something you have already seen*. An array gives you cheap access by position. A hash table (`HashMap`, `HashSet`) gives you cheap access by **value**: "have I seen this number?", "how many times did this letter occur?", "which index held the complement?". Trading memory for lookup speed turns many O(n²) double loops into one O(n) pass.

Reach for hashing when the problem says: *duplicate*, *anagram*, *frequency*, *pair that sums to*, *group by*, *first unique*, *consecutive*. Reach for a plain array (instead of a map) when the keys are small and dense, such as lowercase letters: `int[26]` is faster and simpler than `HashMap<Character,Integer>`.

| Operation | `HashMap` / `HashSet` | Array of size n |
|---|---|---|
| Insert, lookup, remove by key | O(1) average | Lookup by index O(1) |
| Iterate | O(n), no guaranteed order | O(n), index order |
| Extra memory | O(n) | O(n) |
"Without sorting", "in O(n) time", "count the number of", "group together" almost always mean a hash table or a counting array.
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: `HashMap.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` counts in one line. `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>())` builds groups. A `HashSet` answers "seen before?" with the return value of `add`. When the key is a *collection of values* (a sorted word, a count signature), turn it into a `String` or `List`: **arrays do not compare by content as map keys**.

blocks.title: ArraysHashing.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** Every method makes *one pass* and lets the table do the searching. In `longestConsecutive` the inner `while` looks like a nested loop, but each number is visited by the `while` at most once overall, because only run starts enter it: that is why the total stays O(n).

- **Arrays as keys.** `map.put(new int[]{1,2}, ...)` hashes the *reference*, not the contents. Use a `String`, a `List<Integer>`, or a record.
- **`Integer` equality.** `a == b` on two `Integer` objects is only reliable between -128 and 127. Use `equals`.
- **Iteration order.** `HashMap` has no guaranteed order. If the answer must follow insertion order, use `LinkedHashMap`; if sorted, `TreeMap`.
- **Overflow.** Products and sums of `int` overflow silently; use `long` when the constraints allow large values.
- **Modifying while iterating** a map throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

Keys are spread over buckets by `hashCode`. Many collisions put many entries in one bucket, so a lookup scans them. Since Java 8 a bucket with many entries becomes a balanced tree, which makes the worst case O(log n), and good hash functions keep chains short in practice.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Why is a `HashMap` lookup O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case?
Key points
blocks.text:
- Hashing trades memory for O(1) lookups: remember what you have seen
- Use `int[26]` instead of a map when keys are small and dense
- Arrays do not work as map keys: build a String or List key
- `merge`, `computeIfAbsent` and the result of `Set.add` replace many lines of checks
- Counting by frequency and bucketing by count gives O(n) top-K

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Arrays & Hashing** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

blocks.title: Premium problems
blocks.text: Problems marked LeetCode Premium need a paid LeetCode account. If you do not have one, skip them: the free problems of the topic teach the same ideas.

items.question: How would you check for a duplicate in an array in O(n) time?
items.answer: Add each element to a `HashSet`; `add` returns false when the element was already there. It uses O(n) extra space; sorting first avoids the space at the cost of O(n log n).

items.question: Two words are anagrams. What is a key that is the same for both and different for non-anagrams?
items.answer: Their letters sorted, or a 26-element count array turned into a string. Sorting costs O(k log k) per word, the count signature O(k).

items.question: Why does the Longest Consecutive Sequence solution only start counting when `n - 1` is absent?
items.answer: Starting from every number would walk each run repeatedly, giving O(n²). Starting only at the beginning of a run visits each number once in total.
